title: Components, prototypes and a clean developer handoff

say: Components, prototypes and a clean developer handoff.
This is the video for module two of UI Design with Figma.
A component is an element you build once and reuse, like a button or a product card. The original is the main component.

panel.heading: Build once, reuse everywhere
items: Overrides: change a label, keep the link

say: Every copy is an instance. Change the main component, and every instance updates. In an instance you can still override things like the label, without breaking the link.

say: Detaching an instance breaks its link forever, so it never receives future fixes. If you keep wanting to detach, your component is missing a property.

panel.heading: From element to component set
items: Build with auto layout and saved styles
Ctrl + Alt + K to create the component
Rename Property 1 to Type, State, Size
Add text, boolean, instance swap props
panel.rule: Do not detach. If you want to, fix the component instead.

say: Amaka needs buttons in 3 types, 3 states and 2 sizes. That is 18 variants. If she made the icon a variant too, the count doubles to 36, and every future change must be made 36 times.
Instead she adds a Boolean property, Show icon, an Instance swap property for the icon, and a Text property for the label. The set stays at 18 variants and covers every button in the app.
A prototype links your screens so a client can tap through them before paying for development. Each connection has a trigger, like On tap, and an action, like Navigate to or Open overlay.
Then a destination frame, and an animation. Around 200 to 300 ms, with ease out, suits most mobile transitions.
Amaka marks Home as the starting point of a flow called Buy tomatoes.

say: Share prototypes with view access only, because a link can be forwarded. Use sample names, addresses and phone numbers, never real customer data. Nigeria's Data Protection Act 2023 applies to personal data.
Install plugins only from known publishers, and never paste client passwords or private data into one.

panel.heading: Protect the client's data
items: Share prototypes as can view only
No passwords or private data in plugins

say: A design can look beautiful and still be unusable. For normal text, WCAG level AA needs a contrast ratio of at least 4.5 to 1.
Large text and important non-text parts, like input borders, need 3 to 1. Amaka's light grey input border was only about 1.9 to 1, so users might not see where to type.
Each fix was one edit to a colour variable, and every screen updated at once.
Her grey text passed on white at about 4.6, but failed on a light grey card at about 4.2. So always check text against its real background.

panel.heading: Check colour contrast
panel.rule: Check text against the real background it sits on.

say: Before handover, check tap targets are at least 48 by 48. Design every state, including error, empty and loading. Show errors with an icon and a message, not colour alone.
Name layers clearly and set SVG exports on icons. Then write notes a screen cannot show, like: disable Pay until the delivery address is chosen.
Finish with a 20-minute walk-through with the developer.

panel.heading: The pre-handover pass
items: All states: focused, error, empty, loading
Errors shown by more than colour
Layers named; exports set as SVG

say: To remember. Build components once and keep instances linked. Use variants only for real visual changes.
Wire prototypes with clear triggers and Back actions. Check contrast against the real background. And hand off a named, annotated file.

panel.heading: Remember
items: Variants for looks; properties for the rest
Name, export and annotate before handoff

say: Now practise. Build your first component set, prototype one journey and test it on your phone, and run a pre-handover audit.
